claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) of fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13) mRNA (NM_001139500.1:c.-32c>G) was found in three male children with severe intellectual disability (ID).
source: We screened gene mutations in Chinese Han children suffering from severe ID and found a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) of fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13) mRNA (NM_001139500.1:c.-32c>G) shared by three male children.
evidence: The manuscript describes screening 100 severe ID children and identifying this specific SNP in three male children, with supporting sequencing data shown in figures.

claim: The 5′-UTR SNP of FGF13 reduced the translation of FGF13 in both HEK293 cells and patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: In both HEK293 cells and patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells, this SNP reduced the translation of FGF13, which stabilizes microtubules in developing neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblotting data showing reduced FGF13 protein levels in both HEK293 cells and patient-derived iPSCs carrying the SNP, while mRNA levels remained unchanged.

claim: FGF13 stabilizes microtubules in developing neurons.
source: In both HEK293 cells and patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells, this SNP reduced the translation of FGF13, which stabilizes microtubules in developing neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Wu et al., 2012) in the introduction.

claim: Mice carrying the homologous point mutation in 5′-UTR of Fgf13 showed delayed neuronal migration during cortical development.
source: Mice carrying the homologous point mutation in 5′-UTR of Fgf13 showed delayed neuronal migration during cortical development, and weakened learning and memory.
evidence: The manuscript presents in utero electroporation data showing that neurons in mutant mice remained in deeper cortical layers at P0 and P7 compared to wildtype mice.

claim: Mice carrying the homologous point mutation in 5′-UTR of Fgf13 showed weakened learning and memory.
source: Mice carrying the homologous point mutation in 5′-UTR of Fgf13 showed delayed neuronal migration during cortical development, and weakened learning and memory.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data from Morris water maze and fear conditioning tests showing impaired performance in mutant mice.

claim: The 5′-UTR SNP of FGF13 reduced the interaction between FGF13 5′-UTR and polypyrimidine-tract-binding protein 2 (PTBP2).
source: Furthermore, this SNP reduced the interaction between FGF13 5′-UTR and polypyrimidine-tract-binding protein 2 (PTBP2), which was required for FGF13 translation in cortical neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA pull-down assays and UV-RIP experiments showing reduced binding between the mutant FGF13 5′-UTR and PTBP2.

claim: PTBP2 is required for FGF13 translation in cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, this SNP reduced the interaction between FGF13 5′-UTR and polypyrimidine-tract-binding protein 2 (PTBP2), which was required for FGF13 translation in cortical neurons.
evidence: The manuscript shows that knockdown of PTBP2 in cultured cortical neurons reduced FGF13 protein levels, and that enhancing PTBP2 binding to mutant FGF13 5′-UTR rescued translation defects.

claim: The 5′-UTR SNP of FGF13 interferes with the translational process of FGF13 and causes deficits in brain development and cognitive functions.
source: Thus, this 5′-UTR SNP of FGF13 interferes with the translational process of FGF13 and causes deficits in brain development and cognitive functions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined data from translation assays, neuronal development studies, and behavioral tests presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Intellectual disability (ID) is defined as an overall intelligence quotient (IQ) of less than 70, together with significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior with onset before the age of 18 years.
source: Intellectual disability (ID) is defined as an overall intelligence quotient (IQ) of less than 70, together with a disability characterized by 'significant limitations both in intellectual functioning and in adaptive behavior as expressed in conceptual, social and practical skills' with onset before the age of 18 years (Dsm, 1994).
evidence: This definition is cited from the DSM-1994 reference.

claim: 1–3% of the general population suffers from intellectual disability.
source: It is estimated that 1–3% of the general population suffers from ID, which is caused by either genetic or environmental factors during development (Larson et al., 2001; Ropers, 2008).
evidence: This prevalence estimate is cited from Larson et al., 2001 and Ropers, 2008.

claim: About 5–10% of male ID patients are caused by genetic variations in X chromosome.
source: About 5–10% of male ID patients are caused by genetic variations in X chromosome, including structure variations (SVs), copy number variations (CNVs), and single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) (Lubs et al., 2012), and named as X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) (Lehrke, 1972).
evidence: This statistic is cited from Lubs et al., 2012.

claim: About 200 candidate genes have been suggested for X-linked intellectual disability (XLID).
source: Large-scale and systematic sequencing for ID individuals and related families has markedly accelerated the study of the intact genetic spectrum for XLID, and about 200 candidate genes have been suggested for XLID (Gécz et al., 2009; Stevenson and Schwartz, 2009).
evidence: This number is cited from Gécz et al., 2009 and Stevenson and Schwartz, 2009.

claim: Sequencing of coding exons of 718 X-chromosome genes from 208 families with ID patients identified 9 novel XLID-related genes.
source: The sequencing of coding exons of 718 X-chromosome genes from 208 families with ID patients further identifies 9 novel XLID-related genes (Tarpey et al., 2009), and yet only covers 65% regions of these X-chromosome genes but does not include noncoding sequences.
evidence: This finding is cited from Tarpey et al., 2009.

claim: Huge difference of genetic background exists between East Asian (EAS) and European populations.
source: In addition, huge difference of genetic background exists between East Asian (EAS) and European (Sirugo et al., 2019), while populations in the Europe and the USA have magnificent databases of human genomics.
evidence: This is cited from Sirugo et al., 2019.

claim: The proper translation of mRNAs is critical for cellular functions, and neurons particularly rely on accurately controlled mRNA translation both spatially and temporally.
source: The proper translation of mRNAs is critical for cellular functions, and neurons particularly rely on the accurately controlled mRNA translation both spatially and temporally.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Defects in translational control have been linked to numerous neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Defects in the translational control have been linked to numerous neurodegenerative disorders (Darnell and Klann, 2013; Gkogkas et al., 2013; Buffington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Darnell and Klann, 2013; Gkogkas et al., 2013; Buffington et al., 2014.

claim: Features within the 5′-UTR can modulate the efficiency of mRNA translation, including 5′-UTR length, secondary structures, multiple upstream open reading frames (uORFs), and internal ribosome entry site (IRES).
source: The 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) of mRNA is the frame for 43S subunit to scan along at the initiation of translation, and features within the 5′-UTR could modulate the efficiency of mRNA translation, including 5′-UTR length, secondary structures, multiple upstream open reading frames (uORFs), and internal ribosome entry site (IRES) (Chatterjee and Pal, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Chatterjee and Pal, 2009.

claim: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most frequent form of inherited XLID caused by an expansion of the CGG triplet repeat within the 5′-UTR of FMR1.
source: For example, the fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most frequent form of inherited XLID caused by an expansion of the CGG triplet repeat on X chromosome within the 5′-UTR of FMR1, which leads to the excessive methylation and silenced FMR1 transcription (Bell et al., 1991; Oberlé et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991; Yu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Bell et al., 1991; Oberlé et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991; Yu et al., 1991.

claim: The CGG triplet repeat expansion in FMR1 5′-UTR leads to excessive methylation and silenced FMR1 transcription.
source: For example, the fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most frequent form of inherited XLID caused by an expansion of the CGG triplet repeat on X chromosome within the 5′-UTR of FMR1, which leads to the excessive methylation and silenced FMR1 transcription (Bell et al., 1991; Oberlé et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991; Yu et al., 1991).
evidence: This mechanism is cited from Bell et al., 1991; Oberlé et al., 1991; Verkerk et al., 1991; Yu et al., 1991.

claim: Current studies are biased to identify coding variants implicated in ID.
source: The current studies are biased to identify coding variants implicated in ID (Gilissen et al., 2014), while the pathogenic non-coding regulatory variants, including duplication, insertion, and SNVs, have only been discovered in a few cases to date (Borck et al., 2006; Bonnet et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Gilissen et al., 2014 and contrasted with the limited discovery of non-coding variants.

claim: Several microtubule-stabilizing proteins (MSPs), such as doublecortin, are involved in axon branching and neuronal migration.
source: The regulation of cytoskeleton dynamics is important for neuronal morphogenesis, and several microtubule-stabilizing proteins (MSPs), such as doublecortin identified from human lissencephaly patients (Gleeson et al., 1998), are involved in the process of axon branching (Kappeler et al., 2006) and neuronal migration (Gleeson et al., 1999; Koizumi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Gleeson et al., 1998; Kappeler et al., 2006; Gleeson et al., 1999; Koizumi et al., 2006.

claim: FGF13 belongs to the FGF11 subfamily and is a nonsecretory fibroblast growth factor.
source: Fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13), a nonsecretory fibroblast growth factor (FGF), belongs to the FGF11 subfamily (Goldfarb, 2005; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Goldfarb, 2005 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: FGF13 might be a candidate gene for the syndromal and nonspecific forms of XLID mapped to the q26 region of X-chromosome.
source: FGF13 might be a candidate gene for the syndromal and nonspecific forms of XLID mapped to the q26 region of X-chromosome (Smallwood et al., 1996; Gecz et al., 1999; Goldfarb, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Smallwood et al., 1996; Gecz et al., 1999; Goldfarb, 2005.

claim: In a Börjeson–Forssman–Lehmann syndrome-like patient, FGF13 was interrupted by a duplication breakpoint.
source: In a Börjeson–Forssman–Lehmann syndrome-like patient, FGF13 was interrupted by a duplication breakpoint (Gecz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Gecz et al., 1999.

claim: FGF13b serves as a microtubule-stabilizing protein required for axon development, neuronal migration, and brain development.
source: Moreover, FGF13b, the cytoplasmic isoform of FGF13, serves as a MSP required for axon development, neuronal migration, and brain development, and FGF13-deficient mice exhibit impaired learning and memory (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Wu et al., 2012.

claim: FGF13-deficient mice exhibit impaired learning and memory.
source: Moreover, FGF13b, the cytoplasmic isoform of FGF13, serves as a MSP required for axon development, neuronal migration, and brain development, and FGF13-deficient mice exhibit impaired learning and memory (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Wu et al., 2012.

claim: Genetic disruption of FGF13 due to chromosome translocation in a genetic epilepsy family is associated with cognitive impairment.
source: Genetic disruption of FGF13 due to chromosome translocation in a genetic epilepsy family is also associated with cognitive impairment, in which not only the proband but also his mother's maternal aunt together with her two children all exhibit cognitive impairments (Puranam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Puranam et al., 2015.

claim: Three male children with severe ID (IQ < 40) were identified carrying the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP among 100 severe ID children screened.
source: Here, we identified a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the 5′-UTR of FGF13 of 3 severe ID children (IQ < 40).
evidence: The manuscript describes screening 100 severe ID children and identifying this SNP in three male cases, with an allele frequency of 2.2%.

claim: The allele frequency of the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is 2.2% among the 100 severe ID children screened.
source: Among them, three male cases (allele frequency = 2.2%) shared an identical cytosine-to-guanine substitution (C>G) in the 5′-UTR of FGF13 (NC_000023.10:g.138286301g>C, NM_001139500.1:c.-32c>G) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is calculated from finding 3 male cases among 100 severe ID children.

claim: The FGF13 5′-UTR SNP was not reported in previous SNP databases (dbSNP, 1000G) at the time of initial identification.
source: The SNP identified in the present study was not reported in previous SNP database at that time (dbSNP, 1000G), but the new build of 1000G database in 2015 (rs757803941) included this site, where the SNP was found in one heterozygous individual from Chinese Han South population (CHS).
evidence: The manuscript states this SNP was not in databases at the time of discovery but was later added.

claim: The FGF13 5′-UTR SNP (rs757803941) is an EAS-specific SNP.
source: Meanwhile, the EAS population of ExAC database also reported this SNP in 2016 and showed that it is an EAS-specific SNP (Exome Aggregation Consortium et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from the ExAC database (Exome Aggregation Consortium et al., 2016).

claim: The allele frequency of the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is 0.13% in EAS population of 1000G database.
source: Up to now, the allele frequency of this SNP is 1/764 (0.13%) in EAS population of 1000G, 15/6599 (0.23%) in EAS population of ExAC, 26/32416 (0.080%) in Asian population of gnomAD, and 9/2910 (0.31%) in Korean population from KRGDB database.
evidence: This frequency is reported from the 1000G database.

claim: The allele frequency of the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is 0.23% in EAS population of ExAC database.
source: Up to now, the allele frequency of this SNP is 1/764 (0.13%) in EAS population of 1000G, 15/6599 (0.23%) in EAS population of ExAC, 26/32416 (0.080%) in Asian population of gnomAD, and 9/2910 (0.31%) in Korean population from KRGDB database.
evidence: This frequency is reported from the ExAC database.

claim: The allele frequency of the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is 0.080% in Asian population of gnomAD database.
source: Up to now, the allele frequency of this SNP is 1/764 (0.13%) in EAS population of 1000G, 15/6599 (0.23%) in EAS population of ExAC, 26/32416 (0.080%) in Asian population of gnomAD, and 9/2910 (0.31%) in Korean population from KRGDB database.
evidence: This frequency is reported from the gnomAD database.

claim: The allele frequency of the FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is 0.31% in Korean population from KRGDB database.
source: Up to now, the allele frequency of this SNP is 1/764 (0.13%) in EAS population of 1000G, 15/6599 (0.23%) in EAS population of ExAC, 26/32416 (0.080%) in Asian population of gnomAD, and 9/2910 (0.31%) in Korean population from KRGDB database.
evidence: This frequency is reported from the KRGDB database.

claim: The FGF13 5′-UTR SNP exhibits an allele frequency of 0.23% in the China Metabolic Analytics Project (ChinaMAP) database.
source: A recent paper reported a large-scale whole-genome sequencing data of Chinese population (the China Metabolic Analytics Project [ChinaMAP]) (ChinaMAP Consortium et al., 2020), and this SNP exhibits allele frequency of 0.23%.
evidence: This is cited from ChinaMAP Consortium et al., 2020.

claim: In each of the three families with ID children carrying the FGF13 SNP, the SNP is inherited from the mother in accordance with X-linked recessive inheritance.
source: As expected, in each of these three families, the SNP of FGF13 is inherited from the mother, which is in accordance with the presumed mode of X-linked recessive inheritance (Figure 1B).
evidence: Sanger sequencing results from families show the inheritance pattern, with mothers being heterozygous carriers.

claim: The FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is located at position chrX: 138,286,301 (hg19).
source: In detail, the mutation is located at the position of chrX: 138,286,301 (hg19) of FGF13 with serial number of rs757803941 in dbSNP.
evidence: This genomic position is stated in the manuscript.

claim: The FGF13 5′-UTR SNP is located at exon 2 of FGF13 and is involved in the expression of FGF13 isoforms 2, 3, and 4.
source: It locates at the exon 2 of FGF13, which is involved in the transcription of transcript variants 2–4, and the translation of isoforms 2–4 of FGF13 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows the location of the SNP in exon 2 and its involvement in different isoforms.

claim: FGF13 mRNA is abundant in both neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and neurons in human fetal prefrontal cortex.
source: To verify the expression pattern of FGF13 in human brain development, we first reanalyzed the published single-cell database of human fetal prefrontal cortex (Zhong et al., 2018) and found that FGF13 mRNA was abundant in both neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Reanalysis of published single-cell RNA sequencing data shows FGF13 expression patterns.

claim: FGF13 transcript variants 2 and 4 are highly expressed and more enriched in human fetal brain compared to other variants.
source: Then, the real-time PCR showed that in human fetal brain the transcript variants 2 and 4 (NM_001139500.1 and NM_001139498.1) that might be influenced by the FGF13 SNP were highly expressed and more enriched compared to others (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Real-time PCR data from human fetal brain cDNAs shows relative expression levels of different FGF13 transcript variants.

claim: The mutant 5′-UTR of FGF13 significantly reduced protein levels of both FGF13 isoforms 2 and 4 in HEK293 cells without altering mRNA levels.
source: Importantly, immunoblotting showed that the protein levels, but not the mRNA levels, of both isoforms 2 and 4 of FGF13 were reduced in HEK293 cells expressing the plasmids carrying the single-nucleotide mutation of FGF13 compared to that of wildtype (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: Immunoblotting and qPCR data show reduced protein but unchanged mRNA levels in cells expressing mutant FGF13.

claim: The mutant 5′-UTR of FGF13 significantly reduced reporter protein expression in a dual-luciferase assay.
source: Furthermore, a dual-luciferase reporter assay also confirmed that the mutant 5′-UTR of FGF13 significantly reduced the reporter protein expression compared to the wildtype 5′-UTR (Figure 1F).
evidence: Dual-luciferase assay data shows reduced Renilla/Firefly ratio with mutant 5′-UTR.

claim: The protein levels of both FGF13 isoform 2 and isoform 4 were significantly reduced in patient-derived iPSCs while mRNA levels remained unchanged.
source: Notably, the protein levels of both isoform 2 and isoform 4 of FGF13 were significantly reduced in patient-derived iPSCs (Figure 1H), whereas the mRNA levels remained unchanged (Figure 1I).
evidence: Immunoblotting and qPCR data from patient-derived iPSCs show reduced protein but unchanged mRNA levels.

claim: A single-nucleotide alteration (C>G) introduced by CRISPR/Cas9 in human iPSCs efficiently reduced the protein levels of both FGF13 isoform 2 and isoform 4 without altering mRNA levels.
source: Compared to the unediting iPSCs, a single-nucleotide alteration (C>G) for human iPSCs efficiently reduced the protein levels of both FGF13 isoform 2 and isoform 4 even if the mRNA levels of transcript variants 2 and 4 were not altered (Figure 1J, K).
evidence: CRISPR/Cas9-edited iPSCs show reduced FGF13 protein but unchanged mRNA levels.

claim: Induced neurons from mutant iPSCs displayed a lower ratio of polarized neurons and increased axon branching points with unchanged total axon length.
source: Immunostaining of Tuj1 showed a decreased ratio of polarized neurons and an increased axon branches with unchanged total axon length in the mutant neurons compared to control neurons (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Immunostaining data from induced neurons shows morphological differences between wildtype and mutant cells.

claim: The human FGF13 sequence is highly conserved among many species including the mouse.
source: The human FGF13 sequence was highly conserved among many species including the mouse (Figure 2A), then we constructed the homologous mouse 5′-UTR sequence of Fgf13 into the pcDNA3.1 plasmid to test whether this mutation could similarly reduce the protein level of FGF13.
evidence: Figure 2A shows sequence alignment demonstrating conservation across species.

claim: The homologous 5′-UTR point mutation of Fgf13 in the mouse attenuated the protein expression of FGF13 isoforms 2 and 4 in HEK293 cells without altering mRNA levels.
source: Consistently, immunoblotting showed that the 5′-UTR point mutation of Fgf13 also attenuated the protein expression of FGF13 isoforms 2 and 4 (Figure 2B), but did not alter their mRNA levels in HEK293 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunoblotting and qPCR data show reduced protein but unchanged mRNA levels with mouse Fgf13 mutation.

claim: The homologous 5′-UTR point mutation of Fgf13 reduced reporter protein expression in a dual-luciferase assay.
source: Similarly, the dual-luciferase assay also detected that the 5′-UTR point mutation of Fgf13 reduced the reporter protein expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: Dual-luciferase assay data shows reduced translation with mouse Fgf13 mutation.

claim: The expression of FGF13 isoforms was impaired in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus of Fgf13 5′-UTR mutant mice at P0.
source: Notably, the transcripts 2 and 4 were enriched in the P0 mouse brain, and the protein levels of FGF13 isoforms 2 and 4 in both cerebral cortex and hippocampus of mutant mice were lower than that in control mice, while the mRNA levels were not changed (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Immunoblotting and qPCR data from P0 mouse brain tissues show reduced protein but unchanged mRNA levels.

claim: Fgf13 mutant mice showed increased escape latency and reduced time spent in target quadrant during Morris water maze training.
source: Most control littermate mice learned to use distal visual cues to navigate themselves to the hidden platform during a 6-day training period, whereas the mutant mice showed increased escape latency and reduced time spent in target quadrant during the training process (Figure 2E).
evidence: Morris water maze behavioral data shows impaired spatial learning in mutant mice.

claim: In the probe test, Fgf13 mutant mice showed less preference for target quadrant than control mice.
source: In the probe test to assess spatial memory, mutant mice showed a less preference for target quadrant than control mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Probe test data shows impaired spatial memory in mutant mice.

claim: The swimming speed of Fgf13 mutant mice was increased compared to control mice.
source: Meanwhile, the swimming speed of mutant mice was even increased compared to that of control mice, excluding the possibility that the longer escape latency was caused by swimming disability (Figure 2F).
evidence: Swimming speed data excludes motor deficits as explanation for learning impairments.

claim: Fgf13 mutant mice displayed impaired associated memory revealed by a reduction of freezing time in both contextual and cued memory tests.
source: Furthermore, in the fear conditioning test, mutant mice displayed impaired associated memory revealed by a reduction of freezing time in both contextual and cued memory tests (Figure 2G).
evidence: Fear conditioning test data shows reduced freezing time in mutant mice.

claim: Fgf13 mutant mice displayed decreased depression-like behavior revealed by a reduction of immobility time in the tail suspension test.
source: Moreover, mutant mice displayed decreased depression-like behavior, which was revealed by a reduction of immobility time in the tail suspension test (Figure 2H).
evidence: Tail suspension test data shows reduced immobility time in mutant mice.

claim: Fgf13 mutant mice did not show apparent alteration of motor ability in the rotarod test.
source: Meanwhile, mutant mice did not show apparent alteration of motor ability in the rotarod test and the social interaction behavior in the three-chamber test (Figure 2I, J).
evidence: Rotarod test data shows no difference in motor coordination between wildtype and mutant mice.

claim: Fgf13 mutant mice did not show apparent alteration of social interaction behavior in the three-chamber test.
source: Meanwhile, mutant mice did not show apparent alteration of motor ability in the rotarod test and the social interaction behavior in the three-chamber test (Figure 2I, J).
evidence: Three-chamber test data shows no difference in social interaction between wildtype and mutant mice.

claim: The percentage of neurons remaining in white matter or cortical layers V–VI of Fgf13 mutant mice was higher than control mice at P0, and the migration delay was sustained till P7.
source: Immunostaining showed that the percentage of neurons remained in the white matter or cortical layers V–VI of mutant mice was higher than those in control mice at P0, and the migration delay was kept till P7 (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: In utero electroporation followed by immunostaining shows delayed neuronal migration in mutant mice.

claim: Re-expression of wildtype Fgf13 partially rescued the migratory defect of mutant mice.
source: When the plasmid expressing wildtype Fgf13 was co-transfected, the migratory defect of mutant mice could be partially rescued by addition of FGF13 (Figure 3B), indicating a critical role of FGF13 in regulating neuronal migration.
evidence: Rescue experiments with wildtype Fgf13 show partial restoration of normal migration patterns.

claim: The vast majority of cortical neurons in both control and Fgf13 mutant mice migrated into layers II–IV at P14.
source: Notably, the vast majority of cortical neurons in both control mice and mutant mice migrated into layers II–IV at P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting potential compensation in neuronal migration in mutant mice at late phase of development.
evidence: Immunostaining at P14 shows similar distribution of neurons in wildtype and mutant mice.

claim: In Fgf13 mutant mice, Cux1-positive neurons were distributed in both layers II–IV and mislocation throughout layers V–VI, with reduced thickness of superficial cortical layer at P0 but compensated at P7.
source: In mutant mice, Cux1-positive neurons were distributed in both layers II–IV and mislocated throughout layers V–VI, with reduced thickness of superficial cortical layer at P0 but compensated at P7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Cux1 immunostaining shows laminar defects at P0 that are compensated by P7.

claim: DIV4 cortical neurons cultured from Fgf13 mutant mice showed lower ratio of polarized morphology and displayed more axon branches compared to wildtype mice.
source: Most neurons from wildtype mice extended a unique primary axon, while nearly 40% of neurons from mutant mice did not develop into polarized neurons (Figure 3C, D). The total number of axon branches was also increased in the neurons from mutant mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Immunostaining of cultured neurons shows morphological defects in mutant neurons.

claim: The abnormal neuronal polarization and axon branching of Fgf13 mutant mice were able to be reversed by the expression of FGF13.
source: Furthermore, the abnormal neuronal polarization and axon branching of mutant mice were able to be reversed by the expression of FGF13, indicating a critical role of FGF13 in regulating axon branching (Figure 3D).
evidence: Rescue experiments with FGF13 expression show restoration of normal neuronal morphology.

claim: Axon arbors projected to the contralateral somatosensory cortex displayed higher intensity in Fgf13 mutant mice than in wildtype mice at P7.
source: However, axon arbors projected to the contralateral somatosensory cortex displayed higher intensity in mutant mice than that in wildtype mice, suggesting more complex axon projection induced by the Fgf13 mutation (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: In utero electroporation with GFP followed by imaging shows increased axon complexity in mutant mice.

claim: Axons in Fgf13 mutant mice projected to additional cortical regions including secondary somatosensory cortex (S2).
source: The axons also projected to additional cortical regions including secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) in mutant mice (Figure 3E), consistent with the increased number of axon branches in cultured neurons induced by the Fgf13 mutation (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Imaging of brain sections shows axon projections to S2 in mutant but not wildtype mice.

claim: The complexity of contralateral axon projection was increased at P14 in Fgf13 mutant mice.
source: Additionally, the complexity of contralateral axon projection was also remained to be increased at P14 in the mutant mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Imaging at P14 shows sustained increase in axon complexity in mutant mice.

claim: The spine density of either basal or apical dendrites was decreased in Fgf13 mutant mice in both S1 and CA1 hippocampal regions.
source: The spine density of either basal or apical dendrites was decreased in Fgf13 mutant mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Golgi staining shows reduced dendritic spine density in mutant mice.

claim: The polysome-to-monosome ratios of cortex in wildtype and Fgf13 mutant mice were similar, suggesting that global translation activity was not changed.
source: The polysome-to-monosome ratios of cortex in wildtype and mutant mice were similar in the polysome profiling chart, in which the amount of ribosomal RNAs in different fractions was detected by UV detector at 254 nm, suggesting that the global translation activity of mutant mice was not changed (Figure 4A).
evidence: Polysome profiling UV absorption profiles show similar overall translation in wildtype and mutant mice.

claim: The ratio of FGF13 mRNA in ribosomes (monosome plus polysomes) divided by free RNA was not changed in Fgf13 mutant mice.
source: The ratio of FGF13 or GAPDH mRNA in ribosomes (monosome plus polysomes) divided by free RNA was not changed, implying that total translating mRNAs were not changed in mutant mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantification of mRNA in different polysome fractions shows no change in total ribosome-associated mRNA.

claim: The ratio of FGF13 mRNA in heavy fractions (≥5 polysomes) versus light fractions (2–4 polysomes) was lower in Fgf13 mutant mice compared to wildtype mice.
source: Importantly, the ratio of FGF13 mRNA in the heavy fractions (≥5 polysomes) versus that in the light fractions (2–4 polysomes) was lower in mutant mice compared to that in wildtype mice, while the ratio of GAPDH mRNA remained unchanged in mutant mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantification of mRNA distribution across polysome fractions shows reduced heavy polysome association for FGF13 mRNA in mutant mice.

claim: FGF13 mRNA showed less association with heavy polysomes in the cortex of Fgf13 mutant mice, but the total mRNA level of FGF13 was not altered.
source: Additionally, the semi-quantitative PCR following the polysome profiling (Tahmasebi et al., 2014) also detected that FGF13 mRNA showed less association with heavy polysomes in the cortex of mutant mice, but the total mRNA level of FGF13 was not altered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Semi-quantitative PCR of polysome fractions confirms reduced heavy polysome association without change in total mRNA.

claim: The 5′-UTR point mutation impaired the binding of FGF13 mRNA with translating ribosomes.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR showed that the amount of HA-immunoprecipitated FGF13 mRNA was decreased in HEK293 cells expressing the mouse Fgf13 5′-UTR mutant compared to the wildtype (Figure 4E).
evidence: RNA immunoprecipitation with HA-RPL22 shows reduced FGF13 mRNA binding to ribosomes with mutant 5′-UTR.

claim: The 5′-UTR of FGF13 had no IRES activity.
source: Although the IRES could stimulate the cap-independent translation on RNA, we found that the 5′-UTR of FGF13 had no IRES activity with the dual-luciferase analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Dual-luciferase assay with IRES reporter construct shows no IRES activity for FGF13 5′-UTR.

claim: The point mutation of FGF13 did not alter the secondary structure of the core 5′-UTR mRNA by online prediction.
source: However, the point mutation of FGF13 did not alter the secondary structure of the core 5′-UTR mRNA by online prediction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Computational prediction of RNA secondary structure shows no change with the mutation.

claim: None of the uORFs was found in the FGF13 transcripts using website prediction.
source: None of the uORFs was found in the FGF13 transcripts using the website prediction.
evidence: Computational analysis found no upstream ORFs in FGF13 5′-UTR.

claim: PTBP1 displayed the highest enrichment in RNA pull-down assay with wildtype FGF13 5′-UTR and a clearly higher affinity with the wildtype sequence than the mutant one.
source: Notably, PTBP1 displayed the highest enrichment and a clearly higher affinity with the wildtype sequence than the mutant one (5'-biotin-CUUCCGUCUUGUGAGCG-CUUCCGUCUUGUGAGCG-CUUCCGUCUUGUGAGCG-3'), while some other proteins including MATR3 had equivalent binding affinity with both wildtype and mutant sequences (Figure 5B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis of RNA pull-down shows PTBP1 as top hit with differential binding to wildtype vs mutant RNA.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the binding of wildtype sequence of synthesized RNA with PTBP1 and a decrease in the binding affinity of PTBP1 with the mutant sequence in HEK293 cells.
source: Immunoblotting also confirmed the binding of wildtype sequence of synthesized RNA with PTBP1 and a decrease in the binding affinity of PTBP1 with the mutant sequence of synthesized RNA in HEK293 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Immunoblotting of RNA pull-down samples confirms reduced PTBP1 binding to mutant RNA.

claim: Purified PTBP1 protein showed a lower binding affinity with the mutant sequence of FGF13 5′-UTR than with the wildtype one.
source: Moreover, the purified PTBP1 protein also showed a lower binding affinity with the mutant sequence of FGF13 5′-UTR than that with the wildtype one (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct binding assay with purified PTBP1 protein shows reduced binding to mutant RNA.

claim: PTBP2 is the neural paralog of PTBP1 and is increased with neuronal differentiation.
source: PTBP2 (also named as nPTB or brPTB) has been reported to be the neural paralog of PTBP1 and is increased with the neuronal differentiation (Keppetipola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Keppetipola et al., 2012.

claim: PTBP2 mRNA is more enriched than PTBP1 mRNA in neurons of human fetal prefrontal cortex.
source: Reanalysis of the published data of single-cell RNA sequencing from human fetal prefrontal cortex showed that both PTBP1 and PTBP2 mRNAs were abundant in human NPCs, but PTBP2 mRNA was more enriched than PTBP1 mRNA in neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: Reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data shows differential expression patterns of PTBP1 and PTBP2.

claim: PTBP2 expression was increased at E14–E16, but decreased at P0 to a certain level that remained at least to P8 in mouse cerebral cortex.
source: The PTBP2 expression was increased at E14–E16, but decreased at P0 to a certain level that remained at least to P8 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Immunoblotting of mouse cortex at different developmental stages shows PTBP2 expression pattern.

claim: PTBP2 mRNA was abundant in induced NPCs compared with HEK293 cells and human iPSCs, while PTBP1 was largely decreased in NPCs.
source: The PTBP2 mRNA was also abundant in the induced NPCs compared with that in HEK293 cells and human iPSCs, while PTBP1 was largely decreased in NPCs (Figure 5G).
evidence: qPCR data shows differential expression of PTBP1 and PTBP2 across different cell types.

claim: The synthesized mutation-carrying RNA of Fgf13 displayed a lower binding affinity with PTBP2 in cell extract from mouse cortex compared to the wildtype one.
source: Notably, the synthesized mutation-carrying RNA of Fgf13 (5'-biotin-CUUCCUUCUCGUGGACG-CUUCCUUCUCGUGGACG-CUUCCUUCUCGUGGACG-3') displayed a lower binding affinity with PTBP2 in cell extract from mouse cortex compared to that of the wildtype one (5'-biotin-CUUCCUUCUCCUGGACG-CUUCCUUCUCCUGGACG-CUUCCUUCUCCUGGACG-3') (Figure 5H).
evidence: RNA pull-down with mouse cortex extract shows reduced PTBP2 binding to mutant Fgf13 RNA.

claim: Purified human PTBP2 could bind to the wildtype sequence of synthesized RNA, and the point mutation largely hampered this binding affinity.
source: Consistently, immunoblotting showed that the purified PTBP2 could bind to the wildtype sequence of synthesized RNA, and the point mutation largely hampered this binding affinity (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct binding assay with purified PTBP2 protein shows reduced binding to mutant RNA.

claim: The highly enriched FGF13 mRNA by PTBP2 in wildtype iPSCs was largely decreased in mutant iPSCs with FGF13 5′-UTR SNP.
source: The highly enriched (approximately fivefolds) FGF13 mRNA by PTBP2 in wildtype iPSCs was largely decreased in mutant iPSCs with FGF13 5′-UTR SNP (Figure 5L).
evidence: UV-RIP experiment in iPSCs shows reduced PTBP2 binding to endogenous FGF13 mRNA with the mutation.

claim: Knockdown of PTBP1 in HEK293 cells reduced the protein level of wildtype FGF13 reporter while the mRNA level was not reduced.
source: Knockdown of highly expressed PTBP1 in HEK293 cells (Figure 6A) with small interference RNA (siRNA) indeed reduced the protein level of wildtype FGF13 reporter, while the mRNA level was not reduced (Figure 6A), suggesting that PTBP1 is required for FGF13 translation.
evidence: siRNA knockdown experiment shows PTBP1 is required for FGF13 protein expression.

claim: The FGF13 level was decreased in cultured cortical neurons when PTBP2 was knocked down.
source: Immunoblotting showed that the FGF13 level was decreased in cultured cortical neurons when PTBP2 was knocked down (Figure 6B).
evidence: siRNA knockdown experiment shows PTBP2 is required for FGF13 protein expression in neurons.

claim: Exogenous MS2-FGF13 mRNA exhibited increased binding to Flag-MCP-PTBP2 in HEK293 cells.
source: RIP experiments detected that the exogenous MS2-FGF13 mRNA exhibited an increased binding to MCP-PTBP2 in HEK293 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: RIP experiment with MS2/MCP system shows enhanced binding between PTBP2 and FGF13 mRNA.

claim: MCP-PTBP2 increased the protein level of FGF13 in HEK293 cells compared with PTBP2 alone.
source: At the same time, MCP-PTBP2 increased the protein level of FGF13 in HEK293 cells compared with PTBP2 alone (Figure 6E), suggesting that the enhanced binding of PTBP2 to FGF13 5′-UTR is able to increase the protein translation.
evidence: Immunoblotting shows that enhancing PTBP2 binding to FGF13 mRNA increases protein expression.

claim: The level of mPUF-PTBP2 pull-downed by the synthesized mutant RNA was increased to the level similar to that by the synthesized wildtype RNA.
source: The level of mPUF-PTBP2 pull-downed by the synthesized mutant RNA was increased to the level similar to that by the synthesized wildtype RNA, while wPUF-PTBP2 could only partially bind with the synthesized mutation-carrying RNA (~65% of binding with the synthesized wildtype RNA) (Figure 6G), suggesting that the engineered mPUF-PTBP2 increases the binding of PTBP2 with mutant Fgf13 5′-UTR.
evidence: RNA pull-down assay shows that mPUF-PTBP2 rescues binding to mutant RNA.

claim: The expression of mPUF-PTBP2 increased the FGF13 protein level in the cortical neurons of Fgf13 mutant mice, although wPUF-PTBP2 had no effect on FGF13 expression.
source: Immunoblotting showed that the expression of mPUF-PTBP2 increased the FGF13 protein level in the cortical neurons of mutant mice, although wPUF-PTBP2 had no effect on FGF13 expression (Figure 6H).
evidence: Lentiviral expression of mPUF-PTBP2 in mutant neurons rescues FGF13 protein levels.

claim: Expressing mPUF-PTBP2 but not wPUF-PTBP2 could rescue the decreased polarity and increased axon branching defects in cortical neurons cultured from Fgf13 mutant mice.
source: Cortical neurons cultured from Fgf13 mutant mice had decreased polarity and increased axon branching, while expressing mPUF-PTBP2 but not wPUF-PTBP2 could rescue these defects (Figure 6I), consistent with the finding that the expression of mPUF-PTBP2 rather than wPUF-PTBP2 increased the FGF13 protein level in cortical neurons of mutant mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: Immunostaining of neurons shows that mPUF-PTBP2 rescues morphological defects in mutant neurons.

claim: PTBP2 is distributed in both nucleus and cytoplasm of neurons cultured from mouse cerebral cortex at P0.
source: PTBP2 was distributed in both nucleus and cytoplasm of neurons cultured from mouse cerebral cortex at P0 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunoblotting of nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions shows PTBP2 in both compartments.

claim: Children 1 and 3 carrying the FGF13 SNP displayed mild to profound defects in adaptive behaviors through the test of Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales.
source: Children 1 and 3 displayed mild to profound defects in adaptive behaviors through the test of Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales.
evidence: Clinical assessment data from ID patients.

claim: All three ID children carrying the FGF13 SNP showed problems in speaking.
source: They all showed problems in speaking, and children 1 and 2 could only learn to make simple monosyllabic sounds, while child 3 was milder and could go to normal primary school at first and second grades after training.
evidence: Clinical assessment data from ID patients.

claim: Children 1 and 2 carrying the FGF13 SNP lacked self-care ability for defecation while child 3 was all self-care.
source: In addition, children 1 and 2 lacked self-care ability for defecation and child 3 was all self-care.
evidence: Clinical assessment data from ID patients.

claim: Children 1 and 3 carrying the FGF13 SNP had high pain threshold and were suspected of mild autism.
source: Moreover, children 1 and 3 had high pain threshold and were suspected of mild autism.
evidence: Clinical assessment data from ID patients.

claim: Abnormalities of motor development were not obviously observed in all three ID children carrying the FGF13 SNP.
source: Abnormalities of motor development were not obviously observed in all three children.
evidence: Clinical assessment data from ID patients.

claim: In normal individuals, PTBP2 binds to the 5′-UTR of FGF13 to promote ribosome entry and translation of mRNAs in neurons.
source: In normal individuals, PTBP2 binds to the 5′-UTR of FGF13 to promote the ribosome entry and translation of mRNAs in neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In ID patients, the C>G variation of FGF13 5′-UTR results in decreased binding with PTBP2 and reduces FGF13 translation, leading to impaired brain development and cognitive functions.
source: However, in ID patients, the C>G variation of FGF13 5′-UTR results in a decreased binding with PTBP2 and reduces the FGF13 translation, thus leading to the impaired brain development and cognitive functions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined experimental data presented in the manuscript.
